resolutions.rationale: Wolpe’s exceptional-suspension claim is identifiable, while his repeated “article of faith” wording specifically blurs empirical regularity with religious faith.
Although Wolpe asks only for a scintilla of evidence, his unsupported claim about 98% of all humans is sweeping enough to warrant the lower calibration rating.
The functions Wolpe attributes to religion form a recognizable line, but the excerpt never establishes why Harris’s moral judgments require a transcendent source.
Wolpe asserts inaccessible order, human purpose, and the absence of secular moral grounding without supplying supporting evidence or argument in this span.
As a constructive move, the passage directly explains what Wolpe says religion contributes beyond consolation, measurement, and ordinary scientific inquiry.
Purpose, moral order, and reality beyond measurement directly occupy Wolpe’s motion-level route, even though the passage does not yet justify those claims.
The passage distinguishes three proposed religious functions, but its key terms—order, purpose, and moral basis—remain broad and insufficiently defined.
Wolpe says Harris has no basis for moral judgment without engaging any secular grounding Harris might offer, making the treatment notably uncharitable.
Wolpe directly answers the usefulness objection by presenting flourishing as support rather than proof for design, precisely addressing its proposed evidential role.
The excerpt moves from nonphysical status to exemption from scientific assessment, although claims about souls or God may still have observable effects and implications.
The microscope-and-telescope comparison only defines the claims as nonphysical; it provides no positive reason for accepting either God or souls as true.
Wolpe answers direct physical-object detection but leaves Harris’s stronger challenge about empirically assessable consequences of metaphysical claims unanswered.
The physical-versus-nonphysical distinction directly bears on religion’s claimed domain beyond science, although it does not itself establish justified knowledge.
Wolpe’s basic physical/nonphysical contrast is easy to follow, but he identifies scientific assessment too narrowly with locating an object through instruments.
The teapot comparison narrows Harris’s evidential challenge to direct detection and overlooks the stronger argument from claimed worldly effects and implications.
Wolpe expressly says he is not putting advocacy in Harris’s mouth and offers a specific interpretive case, though calling the contrary suggestion a travesty overstates it.
Harris clearly connects expected moral excellence under divine authorship with the later rejection of biblical commands such as Sabbath stoning.
The references to Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Sabbath stoning concretely support the historical-limitation claim, while the claim about every sentence remains unproven.
The constructive directly tests scripture’s claimed special authority against the moral quality reasonably expected from guidance authored by a creator.
Showing that later moral standards must correct inherited commands strongly advances the challenge to scripture’s privileged epistemic and moral authority.
Calling the Bible appalling and denying that any sentence exceeds Iron Age authorship are sweeping claims that leave little room for more sophisticated authorship accounts.
Cognitive limits support humility, but Wolpe also posits access through something transcendent within us without showing why that access exists or favors religion.
Harris coherently contrasts revisable accumulated inquiry with special deference to ancient claims, while merely asserting that human conversation is exhaustive.
The closing invokes accumulated tools and ancient sacrifice, but provides little evidence comparing the actual reliability or corrective results of the two approaches.
Harris answers Wolpe’s appeal to human limitation by arguing that uncertainty supports continued inquiry rather than granting ancient religious claims special authority.
The closing strongly advances the con route through public, revisable inquiry, but saying it completes that route would overstate what this largely asserted contrast establishes.
The alternatives and Harris’s recommendation are plainly stated, though “all we have” and fixation in a prior century oversimplify religious interpretation.
Characterizing ancient religious traditions chiefly through child sacrifice compresses their diversity and interpretive development despite the reasonable caution against privilege.
The pro-specific option correctly identifies no separate adjustment and explains that limitations in establishing justified transcendence are already captured by locked move dimensions.
The con-specific option correctly identifies no independent debate-wide consequence and locates the evidential and institutional route within the locked move ratings.
